Q: Best way to find the OS name and version on a Unix/Linux platform A:

The "lsb_release" command provides a certain Linux Standard Base (LSB) and distribution-specific information.

So using the below command we can get the operating system name and operating system version:

$ lsb_release -a

Q: How do I find which two values in a vector a value falls between in R, and extract the lower one? A:

Convert a, b and x to Date class and sort b since our code will require that. This gives A, B and X. Then use findInterval to perform the search. At the end we check that the result is as expected.

a <- c("2025-04-22", "2025-04-22", "2025-04-29", "2025-6-17", "2025-7-22")
b <- c("2025-04-24", "2025-05-30", "2025-06-25", "2025-04-21", "2025-06-24", "2025-09-26", "2025-04-22")
x <- c("2025-04-21", "2025-04-21", "2025-04-24", "2025-05-30", "2025-06-25")


A <- as.Date(a)
B <- sort(as.Date(b))
X <- as.Date(x)
ix <- findInterval(A, B, left.open = TRUE)
ix <- ifelse(ix == 0, NA, ix) # can omit this line if all elements have match
res <- B[ix]

identical(res, X)
## [1] TRUE

Q: How to append lines from a file into new file which name bases on the content? A:

If your 75k log file is in input.txt, you can simply remove the -month-day from the first field with sub(), concatenate your output filename from that (adding "-Foo.log") and append with redirection, e.g.

awk '
  $NF < 2 { next }          # skip blank line (remove if none)
  {
    yr = $1                 # save date before modifying
    sub (/-.*$/, "", yr)    # remove -month-day leaving only year
    filenm = yr "-Foo.log"  # concatenate rest of log filename
    print >> filenm         # append record to year file
  }
' input.txt

Use

Just modify the input filename and paste the foregoing at the command line in the directory with input.txt, or you can create an awk script from the content.

(Note: the $NF < 2 { next } just skips lines with less than 2 fields [the empty ones in your example input], remove if there are no empty files, it doesn't hurt to keep it either)

(Also Note: this Appends to the output files each time you run it, you will want to rm [0-9]*-Foo.log between runs if you change things)

As a 1-liner:

$ awk '$NF < 2 { next } { yr = $1; sub (/-.*$/, "", yr); filenm = yr "-Foo.log"; print >> filenm }' input.txt

Resulting Files

-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   27 Jul  8 23:26 2022-Foo.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   27 Jul  8 23:26 2023-Foo.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   27 Jul  8 23:26 2024-Foo.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   28 Jul  8 23:26 2025-Foo.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   28 Jul  8 23:26 2026-Foo.log

Example file content

$ cat 2025-Foo.log
2025-12-19 18:00 Free: 3001

Q: Can Pandoc convert EPUB to standalone HTML if the text content files are located in the root directory of an EPUB file? A:

Upgrade Pandoc if it’s older than 2.14.2
Buggy Pandoc miscalculates base paths when OPF is at archive root, silently dropping content. Also moving OPF+content into a subfolder fixes path resolution

Q: Typing a decorator on a class in python A:

Is there a reason why the decorator doesn't change the type signature?

Yes, and it's really some mypy implementation details (I don't know anything about Zuban's implementation, but I assume they model it after mypy very closely).

mypy operates on a concept of "symbols" (see subclasses of mypy.nodes.SymbolNode), where available attributes from a module or class are all a kind of symbol. A subset of these symbols that are static references which refer to valid type expressions can be used in type annotations, specifically:

  • Classes from class definitions (i.e. not those built by e.g. builtins.type(name, bases, namespace));
  • Type variables (including type variable tuples and parameter specifications);
  • Type aliases.

Further, when you reveal_type(<class>), the representation of a class's type is based on its constructor signature.

Putting these two together, mypy does not recognise a class decorator which changes the signature, because there's no way to type annotate such a decorator to tell mypy that the decorator is returning a static reference; static references are not even a concept in the Python type system. So, reveal_type(<class>) showing the class constructor signature means that mypy still recognises <class> as a static reference representing a class, and that you can still use <class> in a type annotation.

I don't exactly know what your @deco does, but from the skeleton that you provided in the question,

def deco[**P, T](cls: Callable[Concatenate[Ctx, P], T]) -> Callable[P, T]:
    ...
    def something(*args: P.args, **kwargs:P.kwargs):
        ...

    return something

it looks like the decorated class is replaced by a function (called something). If you use this in a type annotation, technically you're putting a function in a type annotation, which is invalid. mypy basically ignores the class decorator completely to allow you to do whatever you wish here, but the idiomatic way to change the signature is to place the decorator over __new__ or __init__ rather than the class.
